headline: Research shows that most COVID smell and taste loss resolves within a month
dek: In a 2020 Italian case series of 187 mildly symptomatic COVID-19 patients, roughly 89% who lost smell or taste saw complete resolution or meaningful improvement within four weeks — and lingering symptoms were not linked to ongoing viral infection.
summary_md:
## What they found

One of COVID-19's most talked-about symptoms — the sudden loss of smell or taste — turned out to be surprisingly short-lived for most mild cases. Among patients who reported a sudden onset of these sensory changes, **nearly half (about 49%) had complete resolution within four weeks**, and another 41% reported noticeable improvement. Only about 1 in 10 said their symptoms were unchanged or worse at follow-up.

That adds up to roughly **89% of affected patients recovering or significantly improving** by the one-month mark — a more optimistic picture than early pandemic fears suggested.

Perhaps just as striking: **persistent loss of smell or taste was not associated with an ongoing SARS-CoV-2 infection**. In other words, if symptoms lingered, it wasn't simply because the virus was still present.

## How they studied it

Researchers at Treviso Regional Hospital in Italy enrolled 202 adults who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 (confirmed by PCR nasal/throat swabs) between March 19–22, 2020 — right at the height of Italy's first wave. All participants had **mild symptoms** and were at least 18 years old.

Participants completed a **survey at baseline and again at follow-up**, roughly four weeks later. The study tracked the prevalence of altered smell and taste and how those symptoms evolved over time. Of the 202 enrolled, 187 (92.6%) completed both surveys — a solid retention rate for a fast-moving outbreak study.

The design was a **cross-sectional survey**, meaning it captured patient-reported symptoms rather than objective clinical smell/taste tests.

## Caveats & limits

- **Self-reported symptoms only.** The study relied on patient surveys, not standardized psychophysical smell or taste testing, so severity ratings are subjective.
- **Mild cases only.** All participants had mild COVID-19; results may not apply to hospitalized or severely ill patients, who may have different recovery trajectories.
- **Single center, specific time window.** The cohort came from one Italian hospital during a narrow three-day enrollment window in March 2020 — generalizability to other populations, variants, or settings is uncertain.
- **No control group.** Without a comparison group, it's hard to separate COVID-specific effects from general viral illness effects on smell and taste.
- **Four-week endpoint.** The study only followed patients to the one-month mark; what happened to the roughly 10% who hadn't recovered is not addressed here.

## Why it matters

Early in the pandemic, sudden smell and taste loss became a recognized hallmark of COVID-19 — and a source of real anxiety about permanent damage. This study offered some of the **earliest systematic evidence** that, at least for mildly ill patients, these symptoms tend to resolve relatively quickly.

The finding that **persistent symptoms don't simply track with ongoing viral presence** is also important: it points toward mechanisms beyond active infection — such as post-infectious inflammation or nerve effects — that deserve further investigation. For clinicians and patients alike, this research helped frame smell and taste loss as a *recoverable* feature of mild COVID-19, while flagging that a meaningful minority may need longer follow-up care.
talking_point: Did you know that in an early COVID study, nearly 9 out of 10 people who lost their smell or taste got it back — or mostly back — within just four weeks?

paper.title: Evolution of Altered Sense of Smell or Taste in Patients With Mildly Symptomatic COVID-19
